LLM Inference Learning Lab — Stages 1 & 2

30 experiments across two engines and two GPU generations, designed to make a single distributed-systems leader fluent in inference infrastructure. Ollama on Apple M4 → vLLM v0.17.1 on AWS T4 and A10G Spot. From "what does sequential mean?" to FP8 KV cache on Ampere — one chart at a time.

The Question
What does production inference actually look like under the hood?
The Throughline
The KV cache is the master constraint
Concurrency, tail latency, prefix reuse, FP8 — everything bends around it.
The Surprise
vLLM does not protect itself
Every cliff ended in a crash, not a 503. External admission control is mandatory.

1 The question that started everything

Stage 1 was a laptop, an M4, and Ollama. Stage 2 was a T4 on AWS Spot. The point of the lab wasn't to ship a service — it was to see the things production inference systems are designed around: continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix reuse, the prefill/decode asymmetry, the cliff between healthy and dead.

The first experiment was the simplest possible one: send three concurrent requests to a server that doesn't batch. What happens?

The staircase is the point. Each request only starts after the previous one fully finishes — prefill and every decode token. The gap between first-tokens (~81s) equals a full request duration. Request 2 waits 177s for its first token, not because the model is slow but because it's third in line. This is a single-instance target group with no ASG. Throughput scales by adding workers, not by being clever with one.

vLLM, on the same prompt, looks like a different machine entirely:

All five first-tokens arrive within milliseconds of each other. The gap-to-total ratio is near zero. This is continuous batching — the city bus that picks up passengers at every stop instead of waiting for everyone to board. Every chart that follows assumes this primitive works; it's the foundation under everything else.

2 How far can one GPU actually go?

If batching is "free", maybe we should just keep stuffing requests in. The next test ramped identical short-prompt requests from N=1 to N=80 to see where the GPU stops thanking us.

System throughput peaked at N=60 (1,132 tok/s) and then started declining. Per-request tok/s halved by N=40. Zero failures — KV cache only hit 1.7% because the responses were 30 tokens each. The cliff isn't memory; it's scheduler overhead and shared bandwidth.

Auto Scaling parallel: this is exactly why you don't set ASG max to infinity. There's a coordination tax. The right fleet size is the one that maximizes useful throughput, not the one that maximizes instance count.

Short prompts mask the real shape of the curve. Repeating the experiment with realistic ~200-in / ~200-out workloads exposes the knee:

System throughput climbs 25× (44 → 1,105 tok/s) but efficiency collapses from 87% at N=8 to 37% at N=64. The "knee" lives between N=8 and N=16 — that's where each new request starts costing more than it adds. This is the number a target-tracking scaling policy should fire on, not raw RPS.

And once we mix prompt sizes the way real traffic does, vLLM does something subtle and elegant on its own:

Emergent priority, not configured priority. Short prompts barely degrade (+20% TTFT). Medium and long prompts degrade ~85%. Nobody told vLLM to prioritize anyone — chunked prefill just finishes faster for shorter inputs, so they jump the line. The scheduler acts like SJF (shortest-job-first) without being asked to.

3 Quantization: shrinking the model without shrinking what it knows

The T4 has 16GB of VRAM. A FP16 7B model needs ~14GB just for weights, leaving almost nothing for KV cache. Quantization is how you get serving headroom on small GPUs — the question is what you give up for it.

Same 5-concurrent load, three weight formats. The Marlin kernel reads the same AWQ weights but runs prefill 47% faster (TTFT 0.29s vs 0.55s) — same model, better compute. Int8 is ~40% slower on decode and uses 2× the VRAM, halving the KV cache room. All three batch identically because batching is engine-level, not format-level.

So 4-bit is faster, smaller, and gives more concurrency room. The obvious follow-up: does it still get the right answer?

60/60 vs 60/60. AWQ INT4 and GPTQ INT8 scored identically across math, factual recall, instruction following, code, MMLU-style, GSM8K-style, and HumanEval-style prompts. INT4 was ~60% faster on every category. At 7B+ scale with modern quantization (AWQ/GPTQ), "4-bit ruins quality" is folk wisdom from 1-3B-era results. Pick INT4 for the speed and the KV headroom; the quality cost is noise.

4 The KV cache is a CDN

If the same 500-token system prompt heads every request — RAG context, chat history, a function-calling preamble — vLLM only computes its KV once and reuses it. This is prefix caching, and it's the closest analog to a CDN that exists inside an inference engine.

Cold TTFT 0.34s → warm TTFT 0.19s. 1.75× speedup on a 500-token shared prefix; the speedup grows with prefix length. 10 concurrent requests all hit the warm cache with a tight P50/P99 distribution. The longer the shared prompt, the more dramatic this gets — RAG and multi-turn chat both lean on it heavily.

That same caching is also what lets us push much further on KV pressure than first-principles math would suggest:

Theoretical max at 2,000 tokens/request was N=64. We pushed to N=70 long-context (~500 in, ~1,500 out) requests and saw zero preemption — the 93% prefix hit rate dropped effective per-request KV from 2,000 to 1,500 tokens. Throughput peaked at N=60 again (the same knee from the short-prompt run). The scheduler doesn't know whether it's serving short or long prompts; it finds the same optimal batch shape regardless.

The same primitive carries multi-turn chat for free:

Five conversations, four to five turns each, context growing from 182 to 854 tokens. TTFT stayed flat at ~0.19s. Sticky sessions in an ALB are the analogy here — the same instance keeps the user's warm state, every subsequent turn pays only for the new tokens.

5 The wall, and what's on the other side of it

To find the actual KV ceiling we had to fight the engine: GPTQ Int8 (less KV room), prefix caching off, 40 unique prompts so nothing could be shared, max_tokens=1500. This was the test that finally broke vLLM.

vLLM chose queuing over preemption. KV pegged at 100%, Waiting went 0→5, running requests kept their pages, new ones waited. No preemption logged — evicting an in-flight decode (throwing away minutes of work) is more wasteful than delaying a new request by seconds. N=38 succeeded, N=40 squeaked through, N=45 crashed the server outright. The failure mode past the limit is catastrophic, not graceful — this is a recurring theme.

Holding the line at the wall is one problem. Why does crossing it cost so much in the first place? The next two charts explain it.

6 Prefill and decode are not the same thing

Two sub-tests on a single request: vary input from 10→1,000 tokens with output fixed, then vary output from 10→1,000 with input fixed. The result reframes how you think about inference cost.

100× the input grew TTFT by only 1.0×. Decode time was unchanged. Then 17× the output grew decode time 18.7× while TTFT stayed flat at 0.21s. Input and output don't share a bottleneck — prefill is GPU-compute parallel, decode is memory-bandwidth sequential.

That's the shape of the asymmetry. Here's the price tag:

Why API providers charge 3-5× more for output tokens: on this T4, output tokens cost 16.9× more GPU time than input (21.6 ms vs 1.3 ms per token). The same 1,000 tokens take 2.6s heavy-input vs 15.6s heavy-output — a 6× wall-clock difference. Input cost decreases at scale (parallelism amortizes overhead); output cost stays constant (each token reads the full model weights). The GPU is idle ~95% of the time during decode, waiting on memory.

This is the asymmetry that justifies disaggregated inference (prefill on big GPUs, decode on cheap memory-bandwidth-rich ones) and speculative decoding (filling decode's idle compute with verified guesses). Both are on the Phase 5+ roadmap for exactly this reason.

7 Two speed-neutral knobs — one is decisive anyway

Sections 1–6 catalogued the things that do move the needle: batching, quantization, KV cache, prefix reuse, the prefill/decode split. Before moving on to production load tests, two more knobs needed to be ruled in or out: guided JSON output (does forcing the model to emit a schema slow it down?) and sampling temperature (does decoding stochastically cost more than greedy?).

Both turned out to be speed-neutral. But that's where the symmetry ends — one is the most impactful production knob in this entire lab, and the other is a non-decision.

Guided output: zero speed cost, 100% → 0% parse-failure rate

Note on terminology: "failure" here is a correctness failure — the server returned a 200 OK with a token stream, but the stream isn't parseable as the requested JSON. That's different from the server-level failures discussed in Section 8 (HTTP 500, timeout, connection refused). Both are problems; they live at different layers.

Three modes, same prompt, same model:

  • Unguided (just ask nicely in the prompt): 0 of 20 responses parsed as valid JSON. The model wraps the JSON in markdown fences, prepends "Here's the JSON:", adds trailing commentary, or invents fields the prompt didn't ask for.
  • JSON mode (response_format=json_object): 20 of 20 valid — vLLM constrains decoding so only tokens that keep the output as valid JSON get sampled.
  • Strict schema (full JSON schema with required fields): 20 of 20 valid and matching the schema's required-field set.

All three modes ran at ~45.9 tok/s. The constrained-decoding mask costs essentially nothing because the heavy work (the forward pass through the model) is identical — the constraint just zeros out forbidden tokens before sampling.

Why this is the most impactful knob in the lab. Without guided output, you'd build a retry loop: parse, fail, re-prompt, retry, eventually give up. At 0/20 success that loop dominates your latency budget and your error rate. With guided output the failure mode disappears entirely — downstream services can trust the response shape. This is the inference equivalent of API Gateway request validation: enforce the contract at the edge so nothing downstream has to handle malformed payloads. Free at runtime, transformative at the system level.

Sampling temperature: a non-decision for speed

Six configurations — greedy (temp=0), temp=0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5, top_k=50 — ten serial requests each. The spread across all six was 1.3% (46.1 to 46.7 tok/s). TBT varied by 0.3ms (21.53–21.82ms). Greedy was marginally faster, almost certainly because the greedy code path skips the categorical sampling step and just calls argmax.

Why it doesn't move: sampling is a tiny softmax + categorical draw over the vocabulary distribution at the end of each decode step. The decode step itself reads the entire model's weights through GPU memory — that's what dominates wall time (~95% of decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, see Section 6). The sampling kernel is rounding error against that. Pick temperature for the output you want, not the speed you want. If creative diversity matters, run at temp=0.7–1.0; if reproducibility matters, run greedy. Either way, the throughput conversation is unaffected.

The asymmetry between these two knobs

Both are speed-neutral. But guided output shifts correctness from 0% to 100% — it's a system-level capability, not a tuning parameter. Sampling temperature shifts the character of the output (deterministic vs. creative) without affecting whether downstream code can use it. In capacity-planning terms: guided output reshapes the failure budget. Sampling temperature is a product decision that happens to be free.

The bigger lesson for the production stack: not every knob with a flag is a tuning opportunity. Some are correctness gates with no cost (guided output, prefix caching, PagedAttention). Some are zero-cost product choices (sampling). The actual scaling levers — concurrency, KV-cache budget, quantization format, hardware tier — are scarcer than the surface area of the CLI suggests.

8 Where the production cliff actually is

Definitions for this section. A request succeeds if the server returned a complete response — full token stream, no transport error. A request fails if the server returned a transport-level error: HTTP 500, connection refused, request timeout (typically >30s with no response), or zero tokens streamed. Failure here means the server couldn't serve the request, not that the response was slow. SLA compliance is a separate, finer measure — tracked as the percentage of successful requests that landed under a latency threshold (e.g., "96.6% under 1s TTFT" in Test 28). A 25-second response that completes still counts as a success even though it would breach most SLAs. The progression in this section goes: all-success-with-good-latency → all-success-with-degraded-tails → mixed success/failure → total server crash.

Open-loop load at fixed RPS, sustained 60 seconds each, ramping 1→2→4→8→12→16→20. This is the test that tells you what number to put in the SLA.

The transition from "fine" to "dead" spans 4 RPS. 1–12 RPS is rock solid: P99/P50 stays at 1.1–1.3×, every request succeeds. 16 RPS is the cliff: 25% failures (241 of 960), P99/P50 jumps to 2.0×, TTFT P99 hits 0.88s. 20 RPS: 0% success, server crash. SLA-safe capacity is 12 RPS for short-prompt traffic. The alarm needs to fire well before that.

To rule out a slow-burn memory leak we held 4 RPS for 15 minutes:

3,600/3,600 requests, zero failures, GPU memory locked at 14,527 MiB, TTFT P50 stable at 0.225s, throughput flat at 430 tok/s. PagedAttention's memory management is leak-free. You can park a vLLM instance at 4 RPS indefinitely.

The much harder question: what happens if you don't stop at 4 RPS?

vLLM has no built-in backpressure. 4 RPS: 100% success. 8 RPS: 100%. 14 RPS: 54% success and a mix of 500s and timeouts. 20 RPS: 0%, server dead. The 4 RPS recovery stage found a corpse. The error progression — healthy → HTTP 500 → connection refused → timeout — is the textbook cascading-failure pattern. The server will not save itself. External infrastructure has to: rate limiting at the gateway, queue-depth alarms that scale out before saturation, circuit breakers, fast Karpenter provisioning. This is the entire motivation for Phases 3 and 7.
Reading note — why does the 4 RPS bar look bad? The first stage shows TTFT P99 of 8.58s and total P99 of 13.4s, even though every one of its 240 requests succeeded and the median TTFT was a clean 0.23s. That's not 4 RPS being hard — stage 2 ran at 2× the load with TTFT P99 of 0.28s. The first stage paid the warmup tax: CUDA graphs compile lazily for batch sizes the server hasn't seen yet (the same effect that produced the 9.1s TTFT spike at N=10 in Section 2), and the prefix cache was cold. A handful of warmup outliers dragged the P99 of 240 samples. The ~37× P99/P50 ratio on stage 1 vs ~1.1× on stage 2 is the signature. Production load tests typically discard a 30-second warmup window for exactly this reason — the story of this chart is stages 3–5 (cliff, crash, no recovery), not stage 1.

Finally, the realistic mix: 40% short, 30% medium, 15% long, 10% guided JSON, 5% multi-turn, Poisson arrivals at 6 RPS average with bursts to 12.

Mixed traffic safe capacity is 4–5 RPS, dramatically lower than the 12 RPS short-prompt limit. The first burst (180–210s) at 12 RPS handled cleanly — 353 OK, 0 failures — but the cumulative effect of sustained 6 RPS plus burst aftermath overwhelmed the server by minute 4–5. Long queries (P99 32s) dominate total time and short queries get stuck behind them in the queue. SLA: 96.6% under 1s TTFT, 70.1% under 10s total — before the crash.

Capacity-planning lesson: short-prompt benchmarks lie. Plan with mixed traffic, plan for bursts, plan for <30s scale-out. For 100 RPS production with this stack you'd need ~20–25 T4s — or a much smaller fleet of A10G/H100s. Which leads directly to the next experiment.

9 FP8 KV cache: a hardware-gated optimization, learned the hard way

The KV cache is the master constraint of this entire lab — every previous section ended up bumping into it from a different angle. So the obvious next move was to ask: can we just make each KV entry smaller? vLLM exposes a single flag for this: --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e5m2. The promise is seductive: each KV entry stored in 8 bits instead of 16, doubling capacity, supposedly with no other change. The server logs even confirm the capacity gain immediately on startup — GPU KV cache size: 255,696 tokens on T4, exactly 2× the FP16 baseline of 127,840 tokens.

The first question to settle was whether this capacity is real — whether the engine can actually serve traffic into the extended KV space, or whether something else breaks first.

Latency under load (T4, FP8 E5M2 vs FP16)

This is a replay of the Section 8 tail-latency test (open-loop RPS ramp 1→20, sustained 60s each) with the single flag flipped. The chart shows TTFT improving under FP8 at low RPS and both formats hitting a cliff at 20 RPS. But TTFT is the wrong metric to focus on here.

Why TBT is the right metric for a KV-cache change. KV cache is read on every decode step — once per output token. Prefill (TTFT) is mostly compute over the input prompt; the KV writes during prefill are secondary. So a smaller KV dtype should move time-between-tokens, the metric users actually feel during streaming, much more than it moves TTFT. We didn't instrument TBT explicitly in this stage — the test scripts captured TTFT and total time, but not per-token timestamps. Deriving TBT from (total_p50 − ttft_p50) / output_tokens gets us close enough to see the shape:
ConfigRPSTTFT P50Decode (s)~TBT (ms)
T4 FP16 baseline10.21s1.7722.1
T4 FP16 baseline80.24s2.6633.7
T4 FP16 baseline120.27s3.4543.7
T4 FP8 E5M210.07s2.3224.2
T4 FP8 E5M280.10s3.6339.3
T4 FP8 E5M2120.25s9.59109.5
A10G FP8 E4M310.03s0.8911.3
A10G FP8 E4M380.04s1.0713.9
A10G FP8 E4M3160.04s1.0313.0

Chart derived from Tests 25, 29A, and 30A — the same open-loop RPS ramp re-run on each config. Each point is (total_p50 − ttft_p50) / avg_output_tokens, then converted to ms/token. Lines stop where the server started returning failures (no successful samples to compute medians from).

The surprising T4 result: FP8 made TBT worse. At 1 RPS: 22.1ms FP16 vs 24.2ms FP8. At 8 RPS: 33.7 vs 39.3. By 12 RPS the FP8 server is at 110 ms/token vs FP16's 44 ms. Theory says smaller KV entries → less memory traffic → faster decode. So why did it move the wrong way? T4 has no native FP8 compute. Every attention step casts FP8 → FP16 in software for the matmul. The memory-traffic gain from halved entries is real, but the cast overhead eats it and then some. On Turing, FP8 KV cache is a regression on the metric that matters most for streaming UX.

The TTFT improvement that does show up on T4 (0.21s → 0.07s at 1 RPS) is real but not where the value should be coming from. Some of it is faster KV writes during prefill, some is likely test-setup variance — the FP8 run generated ~20% more output tokens per request than the FP16 run, suggesting the prompts and warmup states weren't perfectly matched. Either way, TTFT is not the axis where you should expect a KV-cache optimization to pay off.

Where the KV-cache benefit does show up is on the A10G row: ~11–14 ms TBT, roughly flat across the entire RPS ramp. That's half the T4 FP16 baseline at 1 RPS and a third by 12 RPS. But it's a mixed-cause result — A10G has native FP8 tensor cores (no cast overhead), 2× the memory bandwidth (600 GB/s vs 320 GB/s), and 4× the KV capacity. We don't have an A10G FP16 baseline in this stage to cleanly isolate “FP8's contribution” from “Ampere's contribution.” That isolation is on the Phase 5+ agenda, along with proper per-token TBT instrumentation.

One useful negative result does survive: both T4 formats die at exactly 20 RPS. The KV-cache size didn't move the cliff, which means at extreme load the bottleneck stops being KV memory and becomes compute or scheduler throughput. Doubling the cache doesn't help when the GPU is already saturated on the forward pass — the Section 8 “sharp 12→16 RPS cliff” is structural, not a memory problem you can optimize around with a smaller dtype.

Throughput under concurrency (T4, extending to N=128)

This one extends the Section 2 concurrency curve past where FP16 could go. FP16 crashed beyond N≈64 (the KV cliff from Section 5). FP8 handled 128 concurrent requests with zero server-level failures (using the Section 8 definition). Peak system throughput hit 1,072 tok/s — comparable to the FP16 peak rather than double it — and the extended range from N=80 to N=128 sustained ~950–1,040 tok/s.

So the 2× capacity is genuine on the wire. We can fit twice as many simultaneous requests, the engine doesn't crash, and the throughput curve extends cleanly into territory FP16 can't reach. On a hardware tier where this works, that's a real production win — twice the headroom for traffic spikes from the same physical GPU.

The third axis: accuracy

Latency and throughput were the easy axes. The third one is the one that actually matters: does the model still give correct answers? We re-ran the Section 3 quality benchmark (60 questions, 7 categories, temperature=0) under FP8.

Overall accuracy fell from ~92% to 48%. But the headline number hides the real shape of the failure. Look at category-by-category:

  • MMLU-style (~50 token answers): 100%, fine. Short outputs survive.
  • Factual recall, basic math: partially intact — usually right, sometimes off by a small numerical error.
  • GSM8K-style (~500-token chain of thought): 0–10%. The model starts a reasoning chain, drifts, and ends with garbage.
  • HumanEval-style code generation: 0–10%. Code is well-formed for ~50 tokens, then degrades into syntactically invalid output.
The mantissa problem. E5M2 has 5 exponent bits and only 2 mantissa bits. That's huge dynamic range (good for activations that span many orders of magnitude) but extremely coarse precision (bad for anything where the exact value matters). Attention scores are softmax-normalized — they live in a narrow numerical range and care a lot about precision. Each decode step reads the corrupted KV, computes attention over slightly wrong values, and the error compounds across the autoregressive sequence. After ~50 tokens the drift is small. After 500 tokens it's catastrophic. E5M2 is the wrong format for KV cache — it optimizes for the wrong axis.

The relevant alternative is E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) — the extra mantissa bit doubles the precision of stored values at the cost of dynamic range, which is the right tradeoff for attention. But T4 (Turing, sm_75) doesn't support E4M3 at all. The format is hardware-gated to Ampere and newer (sm_80+). To test it, we had to leave Turing behind.

Crossing to Ampere: A10G with E4M3

We rented a g5.xlarge ($0.45/hr Spot, NVIDIA A10G 24GB, Ampere sm_86, native FP8 tensor cores) and re-ran all three sub-experiments with --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3. The hardware difference is meaningful in three ways simultaneously: more VRAM (24GB vs 16GB), nearly 2× the memory bandwidth (600 GB/s vs 320 GB/s), and hardware-native FP8 tensor cores that eliminate the cast-back-to-FP16-for-compute overhead the T4 paid.

The KV capacity expanded accordingly: 508,208 tokens, 4× the T4 FP16 baseline. Server logs confirmed it on startup. The question was whether the precision recovery from E4M3 was enough to fix the accuracy collapse.

Quality recovered partially. Overall accuracy moved from 48% to 60%. Instruction Following jumped 40→80%. HumanEval went 0→40%. But GSM8K stayed pinned at 10%, and the long-chain failure mode persisted. The extra mantissa bit helped, but didn't close the gap to FP16.

That's an important result: it means the problem isn't just E5M2. Even with E4M3 on hardware that supports it natively, raw FP8 KV cache without per-channel calibrated scaling factors degrades quality. The vLLM warning at server startup — "may cause accuracy drop without a proper scaling factor" — is exactly right. The missing piece isn't the format, it's calibration: an offline pass that computes per-channel scaling factors on a small calibration dataset and loads them at serve time. This is the same mechanism weight quantization (AWQ, GPTQ) has used since the beginning — and the reason weight quantization "just works" while KV-cache quantization doesn't.

Throughput on Ampere: a different league

Quality aside, the A10G's raw performance is in a different league from the T4. Peak system throughput hit 3,049 tok/s — 2.8× the T4 E5M2 peak and 3.4× the T4 FP16 peak. The latency test ran from 1 to 28 RPS with zero failures at every level, and TTFT P99 stayed under 70ms throughout. The Section 8 cliff at 20 RPS on T4 is invisible here; the A10G simply has more headroom on every axis.

Three things stack to produce this. First, native FP8 tensor cores eliminate the FP8→FP16 cast that the T4 had to do for every attention computation. Second, the 600 GB/s memory bandwidth nearly doubles what decode (which is memory-bandwidth-bound, see Section 6) can do per unit time. Third, the 4× KV capacity (508K vs 128K tokens) means the engine is never memory-constrained at these load levels — the bottleneck has shifted entirely from memory to compute.

The cost-efficiency math. g5.xlarge runs at $0.45/hr Spot vs g4dn.xlarge at $0.22/hr Spot — about 2× the cost. For 3.4× the throughput, that's 1.7× better cost efficiency, before any FP8 calibration work. With calibrated FP8 (if quality holds), the advantage would grow further because the 4× KV capacity would let you push concurrency past where the T4 cliff starts. The popular intuition that "Spot T4 is the cheapest GPU you can run vLLM on" turns out to be wrong on a per-token basis once you do the math — A10G wins on $/token, even at 2× the hourly rate.

What this section actually proved

The conclusion is not "FP8 KV cache is broken." It's that FP8 KV cache is a hardware-gated and calibration-gated optimization. Both gates have to be open for it to work in production:

  1. Hardware gate: you need Ampere or newer (sm_80+). E5M2 on Turing is the wrong format on the wrong silicon — latency and throughput look fine, but the model is effectively broken for any output longer than a sentence.
  2. Calibration gate: even on supported hardware with E4M3, the bare CLI flag isn't enough. Production deployments need an offline calibration pass (e.g., llm-compressor) to compute per-channel scaling factors, then load them at serve time with --quantization-param-path.

The way I'd think about this in production terms: the bare flag is a footgun, the mechanism is sound. Anthropic-tier inference systems would never ship FP8 KV cache as "flip the flag and see what happens" — they'd treat it the way Anthropic and the broader inference community treat weight quantization, with calibration data, evals, and per-model validation before production rollout. This is squarely on the Phase 5+ inference-optimization roadmap, on hardware that supports it correctly.

10 The cross-cutting finding: vLLM V1 is autonomous

Halfway through the lab a pattern emerged: several knobs from V0-era documentation were either silently ignored or rejected outright. vLLM v0.17.1 ships only the V1 engine, and V1 is a fully autonomous scheduler.

FlagV1 behaviorLab impact
--no-enable-prefix-cachingWorksTest 9 ran fine
--no-enable-chunked-prefillAccepted, ignoredON/OFF identical
--max-num-batched-tokensAccepted, ignored512/2048/4096 identical
--preemption-modeRejectedV1 chose its own policy
--speculative-modelRejectedCouldn't run spec-decoding
The autonomy is good, until it isn't. V1's chunked prefill produced a 1.02× TBT spike under prefill bombs — better than any manually-tuned setting could plausibly achieve. Auto-preemption handled 42 concurrent requests on a 34-max server (1.24× overload) with 42/42 successes. The price is loss of control: there's no path to speculative decoding, no way to override preemption strategy. This is the AWS Managed Auto Scaling tradeoff — target tracking is usually right, until you need step scaling with custom alarms and you can't get there.

What carries to the production stack

  • The KV cache is the master constraint. Concurrency, latency, throughput, and quality all bend around it. Every Phase 3+ scaling decision targets it.
  • Continuous batching is engine-level; quantization is a memory tradeoff. AWQ INT4 is the default for T4-class hardware: same quality, 60% faster, 2× KV headroom.
  • Prefix caching is the hidden multiplier. RAG, multi-turn, system prompts all lean on it. Cache-aware routing (Phase 5) exists to preserve hit rate across pod restarts and scale-outs.
  • vLLM does not protect itself. Every production cliff in this lab ended in a crash, not a 503. Phase 7 hardening (gateway admission, priority queues, SLO-aware early rejection from the Mooncake pattern) directly addresses this.
  • FP8 KV cache needs calibration, not just hardware. The Phase 5+ inference optimization track is where this gets a proper second pass — with llm-compressor and per-channel scaling factors, on hardware that supports E4M3 natively.

Stages 1 and 2 produced no production system. They produced a lens. Every phase that comes next — Karpenter, KEDA, admission control, cache-aware routing, disaggregated inference — is a response to something visible in one of these charts.
